Cupbearers
kŭp'bâr-ərz
n. pl. (officers who bore and tasted the king's wine; a post of trust close to the throne)
English cup with bearer. The Hebrew mashqeh is literally one who gives drink — the same word rendered butler in the account of Pharaoh's prison.

Biblical Definition

The plural occurs twice, both in the account of the queen of Sheba's visit, and both times among the things that took her breath away: “And the meat of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their apparel, and his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD; there was no more spirit in her” (1Ki 10:5); the Chronicler repeats it almost word for word (2Ch 9:4). The office was not decorative. A cupbearer tasted what the king drank and stood nearer the throne than most princes, which is why Nehemiah's single line of self-identification is so loaded: “For I was the king's cupbearer” (Neh 1:11) — the last sentence of a prayer asking for mercy in the sight of this man. Chapter two shows him at work: “I took up the wine, and gave it unto the king. Now I had not been beforetime sad in his presence” (Neh 2:1), and that sadness, dangerous in a servant, opened the door to the rebuilding of Jerusalem. Egypt had the same office: the butler of Pharaoh who forgot Joseph two full years (Gen 40:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a cup-bearer as an attendant of a prince or at a feast, who conveys the cup or wine to the guests; an officer of the king's household.

expand to see more

CUP-BEARER, n. An attendant of a prince or at a feast, who conveys wine or other liquors to the guests.

2. An officer of the king's household.

His cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the Lord. 1 Kings x.

CUP, n. A small vessel of capacity, used commonly to drink out of.

Key Scripture

1Ki 10:5 — "And the meat of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their apparel, and his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD; there was no more spirit in her."

Neh 1:11 — "O Lord, I beseech thee, let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant, and to the prayer of thy servants, who desire to fear thy name: and prosper, I pray thee, thy servant this day, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man. For I was the king's cupbearer."

Neh 2:1 — "And it came to pass in the month Nisan, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, that wine was before him: and I took up the wine, and gave it unto the king. Now I had not been beforetime sad in his presence."

Gen 40:1 — "And it came to pass after these things, that the butler of the king of Egypt and his baker had offended their lord the king of Egypt."

Modern Corruption

Nehemiah is preached as a leadership manual, when the book turns on a servant in a pagan court whose prayer is four months old before he opens his mouth.

expand to see more

Nehemiah has been mined for management principles — vision, planning, delegation, dealing with opposition — and the principles are genuinely there, because Scripture is not less practical than the manuals. What the treatment tends to lose is the man's position. Nehemiah was a captive people's son holding a trusted post in the court of the empire that held them, and his one qualification for the work was proximity: he handed the king his wine. He heard the report about Jerusalem in Chislev and did not speak to Artaxerxes until Nisan, four months later, and the intervening time was spent fasting, weeping and praying. When he finally does speak, his prayer is a breath long — so I prayed to the God of heaven — because the long praying was already done. Leadership drawn from this book without the four months has taken the shape and left out the substance.

The office itself preaches. A cupbearer's duty was to taste first: whatever was in the cup reached him before it reached the king. That is a picture the New Testament fills, for the cup of God's wrath was drunk by the Son before it could touch His people, and He prayed in the garden that if it were possible the cup might pass from Him. The queen of Sheba lost her spirit at Solomon's cupbearers among his other glories, and the Lord Jesus said that a greater than Solomon is here. The last thing to notice is Nehemiah's countenance. He had never been sad before the king, and he was sore afraid when the king asked him why; a servant's face in that court was a matter of life. God used a moment of visible grief, which the man had not planned and could not hide, to open a gate for a ruined city.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mashqeh (H4945), one who gives drink — cupbearer or butler; from shaqah, to give to drink; the same office in Solomon's court, Pharaoh's prison, and Artaxerxes' palace.

expand to see more

Hebrew mashqeh (H4945) — a cupbearer, a butler; Solomon's cupbearers and Nehemiah's office; 1 Kings 10:5, Nehemiah 1:11.

Hebrew shaqah (H8248) — to give drink, to water; the root of the office.

Hebrew kos (H3563) — a cup; the cup of trembling, and the cup of salvation; Isaiah 51:17, Psalm 116:13.

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — spirit, breath; there was no more spirit in the queen of Sheba; 1 Kings 10:5.

Greek poterion (G4221) — a cup; let this cup pass from me; Matthew 26:39.

Usage

"“His cupbearers, and his ascent… there was no more spirit in her” — the office among Solomon's glories."

"“For I was the king's cupbearer” — the last line of a four-month prayer."

"“I had not been beforetime sad in his presence” — a face that could have cost him his life."
